Since the 12B, E4B and E2B models were added, I wanted to know whether a smaller, faster model could do better within the time budget. | Model and setup | Tasks solved (of 31) | Average time per task | Runs that submitted a patch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 31B, 8-minute limit per task (as published) | 9 and 11 (two runs) | 5.4 min | 81–84% |
| 12B, 8-minute limit | 4 | 6.2 min | 42% |
| 12B, 5-minute limit | 4 and 4 (two runs) | 4.5 min | 26% |

| 12B coder + 12B reviewer, 5-minute limit | 3 | 5.0 min | 3% |
| E4B, 5-minute limit | 0 | 1.8 min | 97% |

**What I take from it**

- The 12B solved less than half as many tasks as the 31B in every setting I tried.
- The 12B was not faster in practice. It writes about twice as fast, but it writes about three times as much per task, so a task takes longer, not shorter. Per-task results are in [Gemma 4 Task Soundness and Local Results](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dmitriigluzdov/gemma-4-task-soundness-and-local-results); speed measurements are in [Gemma 4 Serving and LoRA Verification Kit](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dmitriigluzdov/gemma-4-serving-and-lora-verification-kit). text:
# Q-FT: a Qwen transformer that reads tabular rows as embeddings

Kaggle Playground S6E10 (airline satisfaction, ROC AUC). How each row of the table is turned into vectors, fed into
Qwen3-0.6B, and trained; what LoRA does; and what we found.

**At a glance**
- **0.959795**: 5-fold OOF AUC, raw features only.
- **22**: positions per row (21 feature tokens + 1 CLS).
- **10.1M**: trainable LoRA parameters on a frozen 0.6B backbone.
- **~52 min**: per fold on one A100 (3 epochs, ~920 rows/s).

## 1. The idea in one picture

A language model normally reads *tokens* such as words. Q-FT skips text entirely:
1. It converts each **feature** of a row into one learned vector the same size as Qwen's word vectors (1,024 numbers).
2. It hands those vectors straight to Qwen.
3. It reads the answer from the last position.

It's the same trick vision-language models use for image patches.

## 2. How one feature becomes one token

Every one of the 21 columns gets its own small "embedder". Its output is the **sum** of up to three parts, then normalized to
the scale Qwen expects:

- **Column embedding**: says *which* column this is. It's initialized from Qwen's own word vectors for the column name (the
  mean of the vectors of the tokens in "Flight Distance"), then trained.
- **Value embedding**: a lookup table indexed by the feature's code. Each category, each rating level, each age, and each of
  3,300 Flight-Distance "routes" gets its own learned vector.
- **Numeric embedding** (Age, Flight Distance, both delays): the standardized number x goes through *periodic features*
  sin(2πf·x) and cos(2πf·x) at 32 learned frequencies f, then a small MLP (64 → 1,024). This is the same idea RealMLP uses so a
  network can resolve fine numeric differences.
- **RMSNorm × gain**: rescales the vector to RMS ≈ 0.030, the size of a typical Qwen word vector, so it enters the network like
  a normal token.

### How each column is coded

Vocabularies come from train + test features only (label-free).

| Columns | Value embedding (code) | Vocabulary | Numeric embedding |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Gender, Customer Type, Type of Travel, Class | category | 2, 2, 2, 3 | no |
| 13 service ratings (wifi … cleanliness) | rating level 0–5 | 6 each | no |
| Age | one code per distinct age | 75 | yes (standardized age) |
| Flight Distance | route id for every distance seen ≥ 3 times; rarer → "rare" code | 3,301 | yes (standardized log distance) |
| Departure / Arrival Delay | bucket {0, 1–5, 6–15, 16–30, 31–60, 61–120, >120, missing} | 8 each | yes (standardized log(1 + minutes)) |

Flight Distance gets both an ID and a number because in this dataset it behaves like a *route ID*: each distinct distance has
its own mix of passengers. The ID lets the model learn per-route effects; the number lets it share information between nearby
distances.

### Worked example: training row 0

| Column | Value | Code | Numeric x |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Gender | Female | 0 | – |
| Customer Type | Loyal Customer | 0 | – |
| Age | 36 | 29 | −0.217 |
| Type of Travel | Personal Travel | 1 | – |
| Class | Eco | 1 | – |
| Flight Distance | 694 | 436 | −0.594 |
| Inflight wifi / Time convenient / Online booking / Gate | 4 / 4 / 4 / 3 | 4 / 4 / 4 / 3 | – |
| Food / Online boarding / Seat comfort / Entertainment | 1 / 4 / 1 / 1 | 1 / 4 / 1 / 1 | – |
| On-board / Leg room / Baggage / Check-in / Cleanliness | 3 / 4 / 4 / 3 / 1 | 3 / 4 / 4 / 3 / 1 | – |
| Departure Delay / Arrival Delay | 0 / 0.0 | 0 / 0 | −0.289 / −0.281 |
| *Label* | *satisfaction = False* | target, never an input | |

These 21 codes and 4 numbers become 21 vectors of 1,024 numbers each, a 21 × 1,024 matrix that stands in for a "sentence".

## 3. Feeding the vectors into Qwen

Hugging Face models accept `inputs_embeds`: you can pass vectors directly instead of token ids, which skips Qwen's
word-embedding table. Q-FT builds the sequence like this:

1. **Shuffle the 21 feature tokens** into a fresh random order for every row, every training step.
2. **Append a learned CLS vector** as position 22. It's the model's "answer slot".
3. Qwen applies its usual rotary positions (0…21) and runs **causal attention**: each position sees only itself and earlier
   positions. So only the *last* position, CLS, sees all 21 features.
4. The final hidden state at CLS (1,024 numbers) goes through a `Linear(1024 → 1)` head, giving one logit.

> **Why the random order matters.** A causal transformer sees features one after another. With a fixed order, the model ties
> itself to that one sequence. Shuffling every row teaches it that order is meaningless (like a set) and acts as strong data
> augmentation. In our pilots the fixed order lost **0.0069 AUC** (0.9535 vs 0.9604).

## 4. LoRA: fine-tuning a big model by training a tiny add-on

Qwen3-0.6B has about 440M weights in its 28 layers. Instead of updating all of them, **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes
every original weight matrix W and learns a small correction next to it:

`output = W·x + (α / r) · B·(A·x)`

- **A** squeezes the input down to r = 16 numbers and **B** expands them back. Together B·A is a "rank-16" update to W.
- **B starts at zero**, so at step 0 the model is exactly pretrained Qwen. Training then moves only A and B. The scale
  α/r = 32/16 = 2.
- Adapters sit on all 7 projection matrices of every layer: attention q, k, v, o and MLP gate, up, down.
- **10.1M trainable LoRA weights** (about 2% of the backbone), plus 3.9M in the feature tokenizer and the CLS/head. The frozen
  0.6B weights still run in the forward and backward passes.

## 5. Training recipe

| Item | Setting |
|---|---|
| Data per fold | 559,708 outer-train rows (StratifiedKFold 5, seed 42); the held-out fold is only predicted |
| Backbone | Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base: 28 layers, width 1,024, 16 attention heads (8 key/value heads), MLP width 3,072 |
| Fine-tuning | LoRA rank 16 (α 32) on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down; backbone frozen otherwise |
| Loss | binary cross-entropy on the CLS logit |
| Optimizer | AdamW (fused). Learning rate 2e-4 for the LoRA adapters, 1e-3 for the tokenizer, CLS and head; no weight decay |
| Schedule | 3 epochs (3,279 steps of 512 rows), 3% linear warmup, then linear decay to 0 |
| Precision | bf16 autocast for the transformer, fp32 master weights; gradient clipping at 1.0 |
| Augmentation | new random feature order for every row at every step |
| Prediction | mean logit over 5 feature orders (the table's order + 4 random) |
| Cost | ~920 rows/s, 26 GB peak memory, ~52 min per fold on one A100 (5 folds in parallel on 5 GPUs) |

## 6. What we found

**Fold-0 pilots, 3 epochs each:**

| Variant | Fold-0 AUC | Takeaway |
|---|---:|---|
| **LoRA r16, pretrained Qwen** | **0.960444** | best |
| Random-init backbone (same architecture), full training | 0.960436 | pretraining adds nothing |
| Frozen backbone (only tokenizer + head train) | 0.959788 | a frozen LLM is already a decent feature mixer |
| Random column embeddings (no column names) | 0.958479 | names don't matter (compare full FT 0.958004) |
| Full fine-tune, learning rate 2e-5 | 0.958004 | learning rate too low for full FT |
| Fixed feature order | 0.953546 | shuffling is essential |

**All 5 folds:**

| Model | OOF AUC |
|---|---:|
| TabPFN-3.5 (raw features, fine-tuned) | 0.961248 |
| Kumo-Tabular Large (raw features, fine-tuned) | 0.960378 |
| **Q-FT, LoRA (raw features only)** | **0.959795** |
| Tuned XGBoost, raw features (8 seeds) | 0.959852 |
| Tuned RealMLP, raw features (8 seeds) | 0.959311 |

Q-FT folds: 0.959602 / 0.959070 / 0.960712 / 0.960388 / 0.959283.

## 7. Conclusion

- Our Tabular Transformer works great! On raw features it ties a tuned XGBoost and beats a tuned RealMLP. Wow!
- Next steps are to add tabular pretraining and in context learning similar to TFMs!

**28th place · Gold · Kaggriculture 2026**
*A learned policy controls the first ten days; a planner then chooses what to grow, who does the work, and when to sell.* **Team 吃白饭的大肥鱼** — Gengsr · 醇久 (deepios) · TanPowasd · Tang Di24 [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F130a3b62a9279f9fad630c9ab3b916c6%2F01_three_stage_system.png?generation=1792200935819421&alt=media) **Illustration 01 · From the opening policy to the planner** *Read from left to right: opening actions, the handover of recorded history, and continued planning. From day 10, daily plans coordinate future production, labor and purchases, while the hourly executor compares the next actions using new observations. The bottom strip marks the transition and main settings.* A farm can look profitable and still run out of cash before its next harvest. Crops need care, animals need feed, and workers must deliver goods to the shed before they can be sold. Our Kaggriculture agent had to choose what to produce while keeping that whole sequence affordable and executable, hour by hour, until the season ended. Games involving Majkel1337, DSM, M & M & P & Q and DECEM showed several ways to manage these dependencies. A small cash balance could be enough when a delivery was about to fund the next purchase. A much larger balance could hide a farm with too little production capacity. We built the agent around the work and income still ahead: when each crop would mature, who could service it, when goods would reach the shed, and what both farms might earn from the shared market. We finished **28th of 10,148 teams**, with a **gold medal** and a final leaderboard score of **5111.2**. Our highest-scoring submission was **56720575**, the re-submitted **C2O7** agent. That leaderboard score is a competition rating, distinct from the cash earned inside an individual game. [Official final standings](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/leaderboard) Our agent used a learned policy for the first ten days, followed by a Rust planner for the rest of the game. The opening network coordinated setup actions. The planner chose production projects, assigned workers, built routes and scheduled sales within a limited computation budget. We also submitted a later experimental branch in our other final slot. We discuss its experiments separately from C2O7, because several late changes improved local measurements while the earlier agent produced our best final leaderboard result. This article follows the decisions the agent had to make: learn a coordinated opening, plan production and labor at dawn, then revise routes, purchases and sales as each hour unfolds. The experiments show where that design worked and where an apparently useful improvement failed to help the complete agent. During the final week, we used a Chinese-made PPU accelerator platform for learning alongside CPU simulation and game evaluation. ## 1. Turn production into cash before the season ends Each player operates a separate 10×10 farm, starting with one unlocked quadrant and the option to buy more land. Crops and animals take inputs, work and time to produce goods. Workers move between tiles, carry items and perform jobs; the farm sells its output into shared product markets whose prices respond to inventory. The configured season lasts 30 days, and the final reward is the player's money. Assets therefore help only through income that the farm can earn and settle before termination. [Official game documentation](https://github.com/Kaggle/kaggle-environments/blob/28b6d8af3ce73926b3d0fda1410c1ddd8384ab8c/kaggle_environments/envs/kaggriculture/README.md), [interpreter](https://github.com/Kaggle/kaggle-environments/blob/28b6d8af3ce73926b3d0fda1410c1ddd8384ab8c/kaggle_environments/envs/kaggriculture/kaggriculture.py) ### The same cash balance can hide different farms [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F012c20ee2310fba9e83534b08a6223d9%2F02_equal_cash_different_farms.png?generation=1792201031229941&alt=media) **Illustration 02 · Equal cash, different farms** *The schematic farms differ in crop ages, unfinished work and goods in transit. Dotted connections link current resources to possible future sales, showing which future receipts a farm valuation needs to consider.* One historical game showed how little a cash balance reveals about future production. At the beginning of day 16, our cash balance was **31,771** and DECEM's was **31,710**. Six days earlier, DECEM had sold a batch of melons and bought its fourth land quadrant in the same hour. We sold our melons too; by the following hour we had **7,712** in cash, but stayed at three quadrants. The almost equal cash balances on day 16 belonged to different farms: DECEM had more land, more tomatoes and more strawberries, with work still needed to turn those assets into money. We finished that game with **80,713 to DECEM's 99,340**. The cash gap narrowed by 2,344 on the last day, so most of it had accumulated before final liquidation. This was **CAND2 against DECEM**, episode **115509423**: CAND2 used the same native planner as C2O7 but an earlier opening checkpoint. The two farms reached almost equal cash balances with different production capacity and different work still ahead. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F13ec4980699c4c50aac9fb1d5b23d324%2FA_cash_and_capacity.png?generation=1792201097719483&alt=media) *Data figure A. Cash at the start of each day and at termination in episode 115509423. The lower panel shows unlocked quadrants. At day 16, CAND2 and DECEM had almost equal cash balances and different land and production capacity.* ### Connect each production choice to the work and sale it requires “Grow more tomatoes” therefore leaves most of the work undecided. The planner must find a tile that will be available in time, pay for seed without interrupting feed purchases, assign someone to plant and water it, and return for later care. It must check when the first harvest arrives and whether the remaining harvests can justify the setup before the season ends. It must also find workers who can collect the output and reach the shed before the intended sale. When several projects mature together, those projects compete for the same labor and storage. A forecast price alone cannot settle these choices. A crop may look profitable but consume a worker needed elsewhere. An affordable worker may have no useful task that can be reached in time. An expansion may promise a positive return but miss the hour when cash, inputs and labor are all available. We needed the planner to represent each part of the proposed sequence so that a failed plan could be traced to the missing money, work, delivery or sale. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F0f27398abbd1b5520d70b7b0b70fd84b%2F03_seed_to_cash.png?generation=1792201125033971&alt=media) **Illustration 03 · The work behind a sale** *Inputs and care produce goods; workers harvest, carry and deliver them; market orders turn the stock into cash. Following this sequence connects a production schedule to the next purchase it can finance.* Majkel1337 showed why delivery belonged inside the investment calculation. In episode **110620339**, its farmer carried six units of wool at day 6, hour 3, while cash was only **303**. Dropping the wool put it in the shed, but the land order still failed. Selling those six units in the following hour raised cash to **1,588**. At hour 5, the farm bought its second quadrant and three units of wheat, leaving **495**. Majkel submission **56216119** was playing THIRD FARM CLUB **56326604**. The wool already had value in the farmer's bag, but it could pay for land only after delivery and sale. Both farms can produce the same good, so neither can value a harvest in isolation. A large batch may begin selling at a high price and end at a much lower one. Above the price floor, our own output changes market inventory as it is sold; the rival's output can reach the market while ours is still growing. The value of a crop therefore depends on the production and sales calendars of both farms. Data figure B shows this price response for six products, using the official rule when inventory is above its reference level. All panels use the same horizontal scale. Wheat and eggs decline slowly over the plotted range, while strawberry, milk and wool prices reach the floor with comparatively little surplus. Melon follows a different nonlinear curve. These differences make the timing and combination of production important: each product encounters a different price response as the farms sell their output. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2F5a237c6cd806adcce07eca0b44e5d653%2FB_market_curves.png?generation=1792201154742054&alt=media) *Data figure B. Instantaneous price quotes from the official `MARKET_PARAMS` and `market_price` function, including integer rounding and the floor. Each panel has its own price scale; surplus inventory units share one horizontal scale. A batch settles unit by unit along the changing quotes. At the price floor, a sale credits cash while market inventory stays unchanged.* The market connects the players through prices. When we sell, the interpreter credits our account. Above the floor, that sale also increases market inventory and can lower the quotes available to later sellers, including the rival. Each player keeps a separate cash account; the competitive effect comes through subsequent sale prices. [Market settlement implementation](https://github.com/Kaggle/kaggle-environments/blob/28b6d8af3ce73926b3d0fda1410c1ddd8384ab8c/kaggle_environments/envs/kaggriculture/kaggriculture.py#L652-L688) ## 2. Learn the opening, then plan the farm it leaves behind Strong public games contained repeatable ways to organize the many dependent choices at the start. A learned opening could absorb those patterns without requiring us to write a rule for each one. As the game progressed, the farm became more specific to its own history: crops had different ages, inventories differed, animals needed maintenance, and market opportunities changed. We used explicit planning to compare possible continuations of that particular state. The opening's job was to leave a farm that the planner could continue successfully. Its value depended on the inherited crop ages, animal care, worker locations and upcoming receipts. For example, near-term deliveries could make a relatively cash-poor farm ready to expand. We evaluated the opening together with the controller that would service those assets and use those receipts. Learning from recorded actions also raises a familiar problem. Once the learner makes a different choice, it may reach states absent from the expert recordings. DAgger addresses this distribution shift by collecting expert actions on states visited by the learner. With offline replay training, complete-game evaluation provides the complementary test of how the opening and its later controller behave after the learner makes its own choices. [Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, 2011](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v15/ross11a.html) Our learning code included imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning components, including PPO. The deployed opening used the fixed **OV7 v90** checkpoint; the architecture and decoder below describe the policy that acted during the game. [PPO method background](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347) ### Control changes at fixed steps, with a transition period The deployed agent follows three phases. It uses the learned opening at steps **0–239**, covering days **0–9**. The compiled Rust planner takes over at step **240** and initially uses a transition configuration that disables several later mechanisms. At step **384**, the main configuration begins and remains in use for days **16–29**. These are explicit step-based switches in the deployed configuration. Once the planner is in control, it makes decisions at two time scales. At dawn it chooses what the farm should produce over the remaining days and derives today's jobs. During each following hour it revisits the remaining work, crew, purchases and sales from the state the farm has actually reached. A crop project can span several days even while the route used to service it changes from hour to hour. The transition configuration also checks land ownership. Owning the fourth quadrant enables stronger labor and budget treatment before day 16, bringing those two parts of the main configuration forward for the larger farm. ### The opening network reads the board and the market The opening network receives **39 spatial planes on a 10×10 grid** and **142 global features**. Three categorical planes expand into one-hot channels, giving the convolutional stem **66 input channels**. The spatial planes describe both farms' tiles, including contents, age, available yield, watering or feeding status, fertilization, remaining lifetime and unit locations. The incoming controller needed to preserve useful commitments, service the inherited farm and carry its financing sequence forward. ### Train models on PPU accelerators and test agents on CPU workers We increased accelerator capacity gradually during the final week, reaching **four ZW810-family cards** later in the week. The PPU-ZW810E platform provided a **48-core CPU quota and 336 GiB of system memory**. Learning jobs produced model resources for the agent, while CPU Slurm workers handled simulation and game evaluation. These were different workloads even when they ran on infrastructure that also contained accelerators. The opponent-network training script used the `cuda:0` software interface and trained for 12 epochs. The underlying hardware was a Chinese-made PPU platform. Alibaba Cloud documents the PPU-ZW810 family, while T-Head's SAIL documentation names PPU-ZW810E / Zhenwu 810E. [PPU-SMI documentation](https://help.aliyun.com/en/document_detail/2971881.html), [T-Head documentation](https://github.com/t-head/vllm-sail/blob/cc1b67eaa1bee9a7f375baaef16dff4015650fd1/docs/user_guide/supported_features.md) A learning update still had to pass through the CPU agent before it could affect a game. We exported the model resource, combined it with the intended code and configuration, compiled the agent, and evaluated that executable. Build scripts staged an explicit source-file list, locked source snapshots and compiled in node-local temporary directories. Separate target directories and cached build products reduced repeated compilation. We recorded content hashes for the source and executable together with the configuration, toolchain, runner and evaluation protocol, so results stayed associated with the version that produced them. That separation also helped diagnose failures across machines. One data refresh encountered a Cargo cache collision in the tooling build and a Python ABI mismatch when importing evaluation code. Those failures called for repairs to the build or evaluation environment, rather than changes to the candidate policy. Keeping model fitting, packaging and game evaluation as separate stages let us rerun the failed stage with the intended inputs. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2Fa760eead444a2b22b95dbb253c846078%2F15_compute_workflow.png?generation=1792201429261770&alt=media) **Illustration 15 · From training a model to running games** *Learning jobs train and export models on PPUs, the build combines code, weights and configuration, and CPU workers run games. Version identifiers carry through these steps so each test result maps to the program that produced it.* ## 5. C2O7 was the submission selected by the final leaderboard We kept two submissions for the final evaluation: C2O7 and a later experimental branch. C2O7 combined the established native planner with the OV7 v90 opening, while the other package carried further changes from the final development period. CAND2 and C2O7 used the same native planner and configuration. The change between them was the opening checkpoint, from OV2 v293 to OV7 v90. We first submitted C2O7 as **56687882**, then submitted it again as **56720575** in the final pair. The other slot, **56720565**, contained **cx_blr_o7_r20** with later changes. The final leaderboard identifies the re-submitted C2O7 as our highest-scoring agent. [](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F36551765%2Fb39f79a84739ed778182d613361dd47b%2F16_version_and_evidence.png?generation=1792201443308704&alt=media) **Illustration 16 · The two final submissions** *The upper lane follows the re-submitted C2O7, whose result appears on the final leaderboard. The lower lane follows the later experimental agent into the other final slot. Code, opening weights and configuration together identify each agent.* The earlier agent that we retained produced our best final result. Several changes from the last night improved their target measurements without replacing it as the stronger submission. Those experiments were still informative: they showed how better prediction could stop short of different decisions, and how different decisions could stop short of a larger advantage. Keeping C2O7 in the final pair let both versions compete in the final evaluation. ## 6. Make the chosen investment survive through execution Our clearest direction for improvement is to keep more of the proposed investment together throughout planning. Buying land has value only with a continuation: which tiles will be used, what must be bought, who will do the first useful work, and which later receipts will repay the expense. A promising continuation can lose that value if a later stage changes the work or sale schedule on which it depended. The fourth-quadrant purchase logic operates within a **day 10–12** window. Our CAND2 game against DECEM drew attention to what must happen within that window: once cash becomes available, the new land needs a useful production plan and workers who can carry it out. The land-purchase logic shows a concrete place to improve this consistency. It first creates a trial farm with the new quadrant and optimizes projects on the new tiles. For the purchase decision, it then creates **two additional copies**: one without the purchase and one with it. Both copies are reoptimized across **all tiles**, using the same post-purchase sweep budget. The estimated gain is the value of the reoptimized farm with land, minus the reoptimized farm without it, minus the purchase price. Thus both sides of the comparison can rearrange existing production. The comparison copies are used to make the purchase decision. When the dawn path adopts the purchase directly, it installs the earlier trial that initially optimized only the new tiles, then runs the usual subsequent optimization across the farm. The implementation therefore distinguishes the plan used to justify buying from the plan that starts the next optimization. Preserving a profitable continuation more directly through that transition is a useful development target, along with keeping its cash commitments and worker routes consistent. Land can also be bought during the day. A qualifying dawn verdict can enable an intraday capital proposal once cash is available. That proposal can generate new economic projects with the crop dynamic program, simulate the purchase and evaluate the work that follows. A separate purchase-only branch can acquire land for the next morning when the search finds no worthwhile plan for using it today. This gives the agent several ways to expand, with different timing and funding conditions. Keeping these paths consistent would let the agent compare the timing and financing of expansion more directly. Candidate generation is another place where a specific change may matter more than a better forecast. The main configuration filters out **new strawberry-planting candidates after day 15**, while leaving existing strawberries in place. A forecast cannot favor a planting that never reaches the evaluator. We would revisit such filters together with maturity dates, remaining harvests, labor and terminal sale opportunities, so the planner can compare complete late-season uses of a tile. The daily and hourly calculations should also agree more closely about how output becomes income. A daily production project can look attractive under one assumed sale schedule while its actual route requires another. More workers help only when they can reach useful jobs and deliver goods in time. Improving that connection means comparing project choices using the routes and sale opportunities the farm can actually execute, then retaining the chosen continuation as later decisions revise it. The experiments suggest different tests for each improvement. For a new opponent model, examine whether it changes the selected feasible plan and whether that change helps. For extra work or a different crew, measure the final margin as well as completed jobs and win count. For a refreshed resource, verify that the active decision path uses it. W17, the late-hours package and the unused codebook produced different outcomes at these stages, pointing to different changes in the system. The strongest opponents made these dependencies visible in ordinary actions. Majkel delivered and sold wool before expanding. M&M used an ordered sale and purchase sequence to turn milk into a sheep and land within one hour. DSM funded immediate obligations while holding other goods for later. Our agent combined learned opening decisions with explicit planning to manage the same kinds of commitments. Our next priority is to carry a valuable sequence of work, purchases and sales all the way from proposal to execution. ## Acknowledgments We thank Kaggle and the environment authors for a game with rules we could study precisely. We also thank the participating teams whose public replays let us inspect complete decisions and their consequences. Their games provided alternative ways to run a farm, difficult opponents, and counterexamples that forced us to revise our own explanations. ## Appendix. text:
Team Farmcore, 4th place of ~10 200 teams. Corresponding author: [Iaroslav Pudovkin](https://www.kaggle.com/betmyex). Code: [github.com/B3tMy3x/farmcore-kaggriculture](https://github.com/B3tMy3x/farmcore-kaggriculture). Trained agent: [Kaggle Models](https://www.kaggle.com/models/betmyex/farmcore-kaggriculture-agent).

Our final agent is pure behavioral cloning: no search at play time, no self-play data. The biggest gain came from fixing the labels, not the model: retrained on what the engine executed instead of what players ordered, plus one feeding rule, the same network went from 3 to 23 wins of 24 against our previous best. The three main choices:

1. **We imitate what the engine executed, not what the player ordered.** Strong players over-order and let the engine silently drop the rest. Cloning those orders teaches a policy to issue empty orders.
2. **The whole turn comes out of one forward pass.** A transformer drafts every unit's job and every market decision at once, then a six-layer corrector reads that soft draft once and lets all decisions adjust to each other.
3. **Pretrain broadly, fine-tune narrowly, then average.** Pretrain on 67 top submissions, fine-tune on a single team, and average the weights of two such fine-tunes.

PPO improved our policy too, but per GPU-hour, data and pretraining paid at least ten times more (section 6). After the deadline we found a market mechanic we never modeled: the engine pairs the players' orders by position in the market list, so whoever lists a good first sells it first (+$4 or −$10 per unit). In replays it is worth up to $0.4–0.6k per game against the top 3; we never tested a fix on the ladder (section 5).

| | |
|---|---|
| final model, end to end | ≈5.5 A100-hours |
| training data | 8 583 replays of 67 top submissions, then 563 and 766 replays of one team |
| self-play games in the final model | 0 (the winner: ~8.3M) |
| hardware | 1–2 × A100-80GB provided by our university, plus free cloud compute |
| cost to us | $0 |
| evaluation | ~19k paired-seed games, on CPU |

**How to read the numbers.** A strong agent ends a game with about $100k. The engine is deterministic, so we compare two agents on the same seeds (usually 48): "+$X" is the mean per-game difference in final money, "44/48" means ahead on 44 of 48 seeds. *Margin* is our money minus the opponent's.

| | Common approach | Ours |
|---|---|---|
| Imitation target | Recorded player actions | State changes the engine actually applied |
| Turn generation | Independent per-unit outputs or autoregressive decoding | A draft of the whole turn, then a corrector over all decisions |
| After cloning | Large-scale PPO self-play | Broad pretraining, single-team fine-tuning, weight averaging |
| Checkpoint selection | Validation metrics or local win rate | Money on paired seeds |

## 1. What we imitate: executed trades, not orders

The engine executes a market order one unit at a time. When an order tries to sell from an empty shed or buy beyond the available money, it stops at the first unit that fails and silently drops the rest.

Many top players rely on this and over-order. Replaying the games of 15 top players showed how little of their orders executed:

A policy trained on recorded actions learns these empty orders, while at play time our decoder clips them to the real shed and budget: it is trained in one world and plays in another. The fix works with any deterministic engine:

1. Replay every game, feeding both players' recorded actions.
2. Hook the engine's commit function and log what executed: units sold, bought, hired.
3. Check that replayed money matches recorded money at every step; drop games that do not reproduce.
4. Use the executed changes as labels, and cancel round trips (selling an item and buying it back in the same turn).
5. Compute all input features from the same replayed record, so training and play see the same quantities.

Against our previous best, the clone won 3/24 games on raw orders, 12/24 on executed labels and 23/24 with the feed guard below.

**Rules for states the teacher never visited.** A clone eventually reaches states absent from its teacher's games. Our teacher always fed its animals its own wheat, so its data never had a hungry herd and an empty shed; the clone stalled there, and animals unfed for two days run away. Three rules derived from the game mechanics closed such gaps:

* *Feed guard:* each turn, buy exactly enough wheat to feed the animals not yet fed today.
* *Night-shed sell:* at night units dump their loads into the shed and the overflow is destroyed, so on each day's last turn we sell what would be lost (+$0.5k on average over five opponents).
* *End sell:* sell the whole shed on the final turn.

Six other "common sense" rules (more coops, capped wheat purchases, spreading units out) were neutral or negative. Even blocking requests larger than the shed lost money: the engine turns such a request into a harmless no-op, while a blocked unit wastes its turn.

## 2. How a turn is built: one pass, then a corrector

A turn is a plan, and a plan is easiest to fix when all of it is visible. So the network drafts the whole turn in one pass, then a corrector lets the decisions see each other and revise:

* **Input:** one token per own tile (100), per unit (up to 24), per product, crop and animal, plus a global token. The opponent's farm goes through its own encoder and a four-latent bottleneck.
* **Trunk:** nine transformer blocks. Each head has a learned 19×19 relative-position bias over the offset (dx, dy), shared across layers; removing it cost money.
* **Draft heads:** each unit gets a pointer to its target tile and an action. The market gets an open/closed gate and a quantity per item and order type, plus hiring and land. No head sees what the others decided: unit 3 doesn't know that unit 7 is heading for the same melon, and the sell head doesn't know what the units will drop into the shed this turn.
* **Movement:** a rule, not a prediction. Every teacher step we measured was a shortest-path move toward the unit's next job, so the network picks the tile and a rule takes the steps.
* **Corrector:** each unit gets its *intent*, the draft target distribution averaged over tile keys, and cross-attends to our tiles to see what lies on a contested target. Market tokens get the expected sells and buys and the shed as it will be at market time, after this turn's pickups and drop-offs; the global token gets the expected spend and revenue, computed explicitly. Six transformer layers run once over these 42 decision tokens (24 unit slots, 9 goods, 5 crops, 3 animals, 1 global), and the same heads give the final decisions.
* **Training:** end to end, with the loss only on final decisions, so the draft learns only through the corrector. The corrector reads the network's own soft draft, never the ground truth: a variant fed the true plan learned to trust it and lost in live play.

The policy has 21.5M parameters, about 16M at play time (the rest is a training-only value tower), and runs in FP32 PyTorch on two CPU threads, well within the 1 s limit. The case for this design is the error structure, not speed: the errors autoregression fixes (the right action given to the wrong unit) were only about a fifth of the clone's errors.

**What the corrector actually does.** It changes the target of 25% of units and the market orders in 74% of turns; without it, money drops from ~$100k to ~$14k and all 48 paired games are lost. But it does not do the job we designed it for: target collisions are as frequent after it as before (0.086 vs 0.088 per turn). Instead:

* in 17% of unit-turns the draft keeps the unit working its current tile and the corrector sends it elsewhere. The draft is a greedy "do the nearest job" policy, and the plan lives in the corrector;
* in the market it mostly closes gates: the draft opens 32% of sell gates, the final turn 14%;
* the draft is badly calibrated (expected calibration error 0.21 on sells). It is not a weaker policy but a feature map that the corrector reads.

**Where each decision is made.** With an early-exit form of the logit lens from LLM interpretability, we cut the trunk after k of 9 layers or the corrector after k of 6 and compare the turn with the full network's on 8 640 ladder states:

At play time we also subtract the training class priors from the logits (logit adjustment, β = 1): +$3.2k and 44/48 against the same weights with raw logits.

## 3. How it was trained: pretrain, fine-tune, average

One pooled corpus of many top players was worse than cloning a single team. A clone matched its teacher on 88% of unit actions, while top teams agreed with each other on only 66–68%: a pooled model mixes neighbouring decisions of different players, and its plans stop fitting together. Cloning the top-ranked player also underperformed: reactive players clone cleanly, long-horizon planners do not.

Splitting training into stages worked:

1. **Pretrain** on the relabeled games of many top teams.
2. **Fine-tune** on a single strong team: +$9.2k and 89/96 against our previous model, and clearly better than training on that team from scratch.
3. **Average the weights** of two fine-tunes that start from the same pretrain but use different submissions of that team. Reliably about +$1k over a parent; our best soup gained +$3.3k (46/48), and re-running the recipe with other seeds gave +$0.9k and +$1.1k.

Mixing weights works like mixing data of one team, not like mixing teams. Because both parents start from the same point and agree on about 80% of unit actions, averaging their weights behaves much like ensembling their logits, at no inference cost.

**What the soup actually does.** We ran the pretrain, both parents and the soup on the same 5 760 ladder states:

**How we chose checkpoints.** Whole-turn validation accuracy correlated negatively with money (rank correlation −0.86 over eight versions), and our best validation ever came from a data leak. So we selected only by paired-seed money, in the final week against a panel of 5–7 opponents, since strength was not transitive: some versions gained +$8k against one baseline and lost to others. Our worst bugs were train/play mismatches that never showed in validation; only step-by-step comparison with the engine caught them.

## 4. What the network learned (interpretability)

Shuffling one input group at a time in live games shows what the policy relies on:

**What the product tokens encode.** A sparse autoencoder, the standard tool for reading LLM activations (TopK, 1 024 features, 315k product tokens from 35k ladder states, 4.5% variance unexplained), splits the network's view of each good into readable features:

The feature directions are causally meaningful, though not strong levers. Pushing the milk token along a milk feature's direction, by twice the token's own norm, opens the milk sell gate on 58% of states instead of 3%; 20 random directions of the same size reach at most 8%. A fertilizer feature does the same, 18% → 51% (random: at most 22%). At shifts the size of the token itself the effect is small (milk 3% → 8%). Removing a single feature, though, rarely closes a gate: each decision is carried by several features at once. It is a cheap way to check what a cloned policy keys on before shipping it.

**It found the town's four-turn shop cycle on its own.** Strawberries, milk and wool are sold almost only on shop turns (sell probability 0.4–0.7, against under 0.1 on other turns), and sales rise with price and with stock in the shed:

**The opponent representation collapsed into one signal.** The four opponent latents have a cosine similarity of 0.993: the policy tracks the opponent mainly through the shared market, not through their board. The exception is livestock: buying cows and sheep takes finite, shared milk and wool demand away from the opponent. Disabling the corrector for livestock purchases cost $29k of margin, $26k of which went to the opponent.

## 5. Against the field

Margin per game of our final model against each top team, from two weeks of post-deadline ladder games:

The margins are tiny: in 64% of games the gap is under $2k on ~$100k, and in 29% it is smaller than the effect of changing a single move (replacing one move with `PASS` shifts the final money by a median $0.7–0.85k, with a stable sign for only ~24 turns). Among the top teams, places are decided by many near-coin-flips, which is also why per-move credit in RL is so expensive (section 6).

### Where we lose to the top 3

We replayed our 295 ladder games against the top 3 through the engine, logging every executed market unit and its price (money reconciles to the dollar). Each side sells ~$135k of goods per game, and our selling looks almost identical to the 1st place's: same hours, same batch sizes, same number of sales. The gap is in high-value goods (strawberries, milk, wool), and against the 1st place about half of it is price, not volume: the same units sold $2–3 cheaper.

Part of the reason is a mechanic we never modeled. The engine executes order *i* of one player together with order *i* of the other, unit by unit, and every unit sold moves the price down. So when both players sell the same good in the same turn (a collision), whoever put it earlier in their market list sells first:

Summed over these collisions, that is up to −$0.4–0.6k per game against each of the top 3. This is a replay estimate, not a causal effect: who lists a good first depends on the state of the game, and the opponent would also play differently against a different order. All three top teams sort their sells by price every turn (rank correlation of list position with price −0.58 to −0.62). Our decoder lists sells in a fixed order that starts with wheat, the cheapest good (−0.09), so the network could not compete for the slot. The only causal test we ran: sorting our sells by price gains +$216 ± 189 per game (69% of 48 paired seeds) against our older package, which sells in our order. Against teams that sort by price the gain could differ either way; we found this after the deadline and never tested it on the ladder.

## 6. RL worked; scaling the data worked far better

PPO on top of our imitation checkpoints, with the change in farm net worth as the reward, gained +$1.3k per game over its starting checkpoint (64/96 paired seeds, p = 1e-5), and an RL checkpoint was one of our ladder submissions. Our teammate's self-play runs of ~100k games each gave similar gains.

We dropped it because of compute. Per GPU-hour, data and pretraining paid at least ten times more than our best PPO run:

| | compute | gain |
|---|---|---|
| best PPO run (23 updates of 128 games) | ~2.8 A100-hours | +$1.3k |
| longest PPO run (260 updates) | ~30 A100-hours (estimated) | −$14k against the relabeled clone below |
| relabeling the corpus with executed trades | an afternoon of CPU | 3/24 → 23/24 against our previous best |
| fine-tuning the pretrained model on one team | 1.2 A100-hours | +$9.2k (89/96) |
| the whole final model | ≈5.5 A100-hours | 4th place |

Both final submissions are pure imitation; the RL loop is in the repository as a working tool. Rule of thumb for similar competitions: if the engine is deterministic and strong replays are public, relabel and clone first; PPO on top pays only with far more compute than we had.

Why PPO is so expensive here: at our batch size the per-move signal is mostly noise. Split one rollout of 128 games in two and compute the policy gradient on each half, and the cosine between the halves is 0.06 (−0.01 with shuffled advantages, 0.93 for a control target the policy itself determines). That matches the chaos probe in section 5: a move's true effect is worth $30–400 and visible for ~24 turns, while the final result moves by ±$1–2k for unrelated reasons. A net-worth reward also cannot see market sells: selling turns stock into cash of about the same value. PPO needs far larger batches, which is what teams with GPU fleets ran.

Compute reported by other top teams:

| | training hardware | notes |
|---|---|---|
| [1st place](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745073) | final 10M model: up to 17 A100 + 29 A30 (~7 + 20 on average); a parallel 20M model: up to 26 A100 more | ~8.29M self-play games |
| [pure BC, top 10](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745367) | one RTX 5090 | pretrain ≈50 min |
| [autoregressive SFT, top 10](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/discussion/745036) | two RTX 4090 and an RTX 3090, a DGX Spark, rented Colab GPUs | final model trained from scratch on one Colab G4 |
| us | 1–2 university A100 + free cloud compute, $0 in total | final model ≈5.5 A100-hours, 0 self-play games |

Every pure-imitation team in the top 10 trained its final model on one to three cards. The GPU fleets bought the self-play scale that PPO needs.

## 7. What did not work

* Mixed multi-teacher corpora with teacher-style embeddings: weaker than one consistent teacher. Other teams gained from conditioning on team, version and outcome; we tried only a team embedding.
* Routing between expert models per decision head: gains against one opponent, losses against others.
* Feeding each unit its previous action: the clone learned to copy itself (−$25k for one teacher).
* All board tiles as corrector tokens: attention spread away from the units.
* Sampling actions instead of argmax: money within noise, fewer wins.
* Iterative multi-pass draft refinement: no gain over a single corrector step.

Thanks to the organizers for a genuinely interesting game, and to the teams at the top of the ladder: every one of our models learned by watching your games. This gold also made all of us Kaggle Competitions Masters. Thank you!

text:
## Summary

My final agent (MXFMHF12D) finished 19th of 10,148 teams with a final score of 5,210.3. It is a behaviour clone of the teams that finished 1st, 3rd and 7th: M & M & P & Q, DSM and DECEM. Twelve small networks trained on their replays (and on older games in slots the agent does not play from) each score every move, the agent averages their probabilities, and three rules sell goods the engine would otherwise destroy. No RL went into it, and it does no search at play time.

Four things I measured that may be useful next to Farmcore's and DECEM's write-ups:

1. Pooling three teams that play the same four-quadrant plan beat a clone of M & M & P & Q alone against all seven opponents I tested.
2. Training from scratch and keeping the last epoch beat fine-tuning older networks and beat picking epochs by validation loss.
3. Averaging networks from families trained on different views of the data beat adding more networks of one family.
4. A local test that ranked my live files correctly still could not see where my clones lose.

## Data

For each teacher I downloaded the replays of its current submissions through Kaggle's episode list endpoint, every 30 minutes on the last day. By the morning of 30 September I had 653 M & M & P & Q games, 578 DSM games and 549 DECEM games, plus about 1,900 games from 12 older M & M & P & Q submissions.

Each training record is one teacher seat in one game, seen from that seat. The labels are the orders the teacher requested, with market quantities clipped to 30.

One bug mattered. BUY_PRODUCT orders above 30 were not clipped, so any record that contained one was dropped. DSM and DECEM often buy wheat in bulk around day 10, so until a fix on the last day more than half of their games (316 of 589) never reached training. Farmcore relabelled to the trades the engine actually executed, and that is what I would add first.

## Model

Each network is a small CNN with 898,498 parameters. The board runs through three residual blocks with the global features added to every tile, and each unit's 132 features join at the unit head. The unit head picks each unit's verb and quantity, and an autoregressive market head writes up to ten orders after seeing what the units will do to the shed. Every network trains from scratch with AdamW (batch 256, peak learning rate 1e-3) and a OneCycle schedule that anneals to zero, for 10 epochs at first and 16 later, and I keep the last epoch.

The trainer has three version slots. The teachers' newest games sit in the slot the agent plays from, and older games (Boey's, and older M & M & P & Q submissions in some families) sit in the other two, as far as I can reconstruct from the trainer. The network learns from old games without being asked to play like them, the same idea as DECEM's date buckets.

**Decoding.** Units take the argmax of the averaged distribution, with a legality mask so a later unit sees what earlier units took. Purchases need more care: plain argmax never makes a purchase the teacher makes with a 20 % chance per step. Error diffusion fixes that. An accumulator adds the expected purchases each step and buys when it reaches one. On my first clone, error diffusion and a later refinement were worth 15k to 20k coins per game; the final file uses plain error diffusion. DECEM describes a similar accumulator.

## What mattered

All results are paired: a candidate and a control play the same towns against the same opponent, with a dithered opening, and I report the mean difference in final margin. ± is one standard error. A final bank is roughly 90k to 160k coins.

**Train from scratch, and keep the last epoch.** Eight fresh networks beat my live clone of Boey (23rd) by 11.0k per game summed over three opponents. Fine-tuning older networks on the same data gave 0.9k, or 3.5k with the newest games weighted up. The same eight networks at their lowest-validation-loss epoch gave 7.4k. The agent plays argmax, so validation loss is the wrong yardstick.

**Pool three teachers that share a plan.** DSM and DECEM play the same four-quadrant skeleton as M & M & P & Q: land, hires, a large wheat ring and animals. Alone they had too few games for a good clone. Pooled with M & M & P & Q, they beat the M&M-only clone by 3.9k ± 0.8k summed over three standard opponents, and by 1.2k to 4.1k against four others. Farmcore found that pooling many top players was worse than cloning one team, and they explain it by plans that stop fitting together. My three teachers share one plan, which may be why pooling worked; I did not measure how often they agree.

**Families beat more networks.** A family is a set of networks trained with one recipe on one view of the data. More networks within a family did nothing measurable, while a second family lifted my local score V1 (see Validation) from 0.705 to 0.784. My final file (Final A) averages three families, MXNF2 ×3, MXNM ×6 and MXHF ×3, and scored 0.879 on 700 towns, against 0.847 for my other final file (Final B) and 0.700 for a clone of the teachers' newest games. Part of the lead is selection: the same recipe with new seeds scored 0.835, and the two final files ended 24 points apart in the final standings.

**Three small rules.** OVERFLOW sells what will not fit in the shed at midnight, ENDGAME stops investments that cannot pay back and sells everything at the end, and ENDRUSH sends units carrying goods to the shed before the last step. Leaving one out cost 1,722, 676 and 252 coins per game, summed over three opponents.

## Validation

**Dither the opening.** Days 0 to 2 have no shops and weeds start at step 48, so two deterministic programs play the same opening in every town, and a test measures one opening plus noise. Against a dithered opponent, a null change read −677 ± 1,290 on 50 towns instead of −11,389 ± 2,140 on 15. Seeing 1k at two standard errors then takes about 340 towns.

**V1** = ½ × mean(win rate against a strong M&M copy, win rate against the M&M-only clone) + ½ × win rate against the pooled clone. Across five live files its two copy cells correlated 0.93 and 0.94 with the live ratings, and the final standings ordered my two final files the way V1 did.

**What V1 missed.** Its references are my own clones, so they share my blind spots. In 18 replays against teams rated above 2,550, three of the six losses came from too few strawberries and too little milk, and in wins and losses alike my agent left 16 to 22 more animal-days unfed per game than M & M & P & Q did against the same opponents. In M & M & P & Q's own positions it picks their exact action 0.91 to 0.99 of the time, but in free play only 0.26 to 0.40 of positions match from day 6. The money is lost in states the teacher never visits.

## What did not work

| Idea | Result |
|---|---|
| PPO from an early clone (6.0M steps) | its own sampled metric rose 3.0k; the deterministic agent I ship lost 23.3k |
| Fine-tuning a clone on its own best rollouts | −5.0k |
| DSM's recorded opening, then my clone | −22.5k against one opponent |
| Sending units to rescue drying plants | −1,756 against one opponent |

The PPO run was small, so it says nothing about PPO at the scale the winners used.

## Thanks

Thanks to Kaggle for the game, and to M & M & P & Q, DSM and DECEM, whose games my networks learned from. Thanks also to Boey, whose games taught my earlier clones and are still in the final networks' training data, and to the authors of the public notebooks I submitted or forked:

For teams currently reaching 0.22 - 0.24 on the public leaderboard with single-agent configurations using gemma-4-31b-it-qat-w4a16-ct, I would appreciate community insights on a few architectural trade-offs:

1. Local Verification vs Global Clock Budget
In swegemma, running local targeted pytest suites (e.g., pytest -k with short tracebacks) allows catching simple regressions, but introduces command execution latency. Given the 12-hour global evaluation cap across the private benchmark repositories, have you found that running a local test and single repair loop provides a net positive on the final score, or does the overhead risk timeout starvation on heavier repositories?

2. Context Management under 32k Window
With thinking_budget set around 4096 and max_output_tokens at 8192, multi-turn trajectories (turns 10 to 15) consume significant context. What strategies are you using to prevent context overflow or losing the original issue specification late in the run? Are you strictly limiting shell outputs (e.g., piping to head/tail), or using structured state persistence?

3. First Edit Timing and Tool Budget Allocation
In an 8-minute / 28-call budget, what has proven to be the optimal window for applying the first source edit? Does forcing an early edit by call 8-10 yield better results, or is spending up to call 12 on root-cause analysis more reliable across unseen codebases?

4. Handling Sparse and Non-Standard Issue Prompts
Some benchmark tasks provide minimal context, such as a short title or an issue URL without reproduction snippets. Beyond inspecting recent repository commits via git log, what automated search heuristics have been effective for locating the relevant module without wasting exploration turns?

5. Repository Structure Edge Cases
Certain repositories test examples or tutorial code located in documentation directories rather than internal library modules. How does your agent differentiate between modifying core package internals versus documentation or example files?

Thanks in advance for sharing your thoughts and experiences.
